title: Reservation decay and tenant penalty logic to mitigate capacity instability
creator: Marina Soto
description: Post-incident work to prevent repeated tenant-driven capacity instability observed during the 2026-02-26 incident. Investigation found two root contributors: (1) reservation mis-sizing over time (drift between billed reservation and actual working set) causing stranding and sudden evictions, and (2) permissive burst policy + unlimited burst token accumulation that allowed noisy tenants to consume disproportionate transient capacity. This ticket implements an operational and runtime plan: a reservation decay model (soft shrink of unused reservation over a configurable window), tenant penalty scoring that reduces burst credits for repeated high tail-latency bursts, telemetry surfaces, and a controlled canary rollout with rollback gates.
acceptance_criteria:
1) Reservation decay algorithm deployed to staging; decay rate defaults to 5% per 24h after 48h idle, configurable.
2) Burst credit ledger added to runtime; tenants with >3 threshold violations in 1h see burst credit rate halved for 30m.
3) New dashboards show reservation drift, burst_credit_balance per tenant, and 95/99 tail evictions triggered by burst.
4) Canary rollout to 10% of dedicated clusters with automated health gates; no customer-visible increase in error-rate or latency beyond baseline.
5) Runbook updated and on-call playbook annotated with remediation steps.
work_items: Design reservation_decay algorithm and config knobs (Devon)
Expose telemetry + Grafana dashboard for drift and credit balances (Ana)
Create automated canary job + health gates (SRE)
Update runbook and communicate to support and solutions (Marina)
Performance regression test across 3 model families at peak seq len (bench)
risks_and_tradeoffs:
- Aggressive decay can under-allocate customers who have bursty but legitimate patterns; we mitigate via generous initial grace window (48h) and per-tenant config.
- Penalty logic risks false positives for customers with legitimate sustained high rate bursts; we prioritize conservative thresholds and a telemetry-based whitelist.
- Additional runtime bookkeeping increases allocator CPU cost; can be bounded with sharded in-memory counters and sampling.
- Canary rollout must be reversible quickly; implement feature flag and immediate global rollback path.
